business_outcome: Every contract request enters Legal complete, correctly triaged, and with a named owner for each ongoing obligation (renewal, termination, indemnity, security), so work moves faster and nothing important goes unmanaged after signature.
current_state_work_problem: 81.5% of the 2,400 contract requests arrive missing at least one required field, so Legal Ops spends days chasing requestors before real review even starts. Triage is inconsistent, obligations after signing have no clear owner (320 known gaps), and staff stitch information together by hand across many systems. Average request age is 31.6 days with a P90 of 52 days.
phase_one_solution_approach: Guided intake by request type that blocks incomplete submissions, an AI completeness and risk-triage check that routes each request to the right reviewer, AI-assisted obligation extraction that a human confirms, and an obligation-owner routing step. Attorneys keep all legal judgment; AI only prepares and organizes the work.
building_blocks: Process redesign; Data readiness/remediation; Workflow automation; Human-in-the-loop agent; Controls/governance/risk; Value tracking/operating cadence
building_blocks_not_yet: AI-assisted decision support: Suggesting legal positions or approve/reject calls is not safe in phase one; attorneys must own judgment on non-standard terms, indemnity, and termination.; System/platform implementation: Phase one embeds in the existing contract system rather than standing up a new platform; broad build was explicitly rejected until baseline value is proven.; Analytics/intelligence layer: Cross-system obligation analytics depend on obligation data first being captured cleanly; premature to build the layer before the feed is trustworthy.
required_p2_evidence: Required-field definition per contract request type; Contract request log with age, status, and missing-field detail; Obligation gap register with contract type and criticality; Routing/triage rules currently used by Legal Ops; List of source systems and who owns access to each; Privilege and privacy handling rules for contract content
p2_current_state_focus: Establish the true intake and obligation baseline: which fields are actually missing by request type, where requests age, how triage decisions are made today, and which obligations have no owner. Confirm the corrected root cause is intake quality and handoffs, not attorney capacity.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the guided-intake form, completeness/triage checks, the human confirmation step for extracted obligations, and the obligation-owner routing path, all embedded in the existing contract workflow with a privilege and privacy boundary.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: 12-week boutique-led hybrid at planning-grade $950K-$1.45M. Value framed as an 8-12% cycle-time improvement plus directional rework, escalation, and obligation-risk reduction; hard savings held back until finance attests.
p5_execution_focus: Mobilize only once the obligation-owner matrix, security/privilege controls, requestor training, and value-tracking metrics are ready. Run a pilot cohort and compare before/after on a defined request set.
tower_metrics: Weighted average review cycle time (days); Percent of requests with a missing intake field; Aged and breached queue volume; Obligation-owner completeness rate; Escalation rate; Renewal-notice risk count
required_controls: Attorney approval required before any request closes; Privilege and privacy fence on contract content; Human confirmation of every AI-extracted obligation; Full audit trail of who changed what and when; Access controls per source system; Segregation of AI-prepared work from final legal sign-off
client_stakeholders: Deputy General Counsel; Legal Operations Lead; Procurement; Finance Controls; IT/Data owner; Information Security; OpCo requestor representatives
what_good_looks_like: Requests arrive complete and pre-triaged, attorneys spend time on judgment rather than chasing fields, every live obligation has a named owner, and Legal, Finance, and the OpCos see the same trusted status and value picture.
biggest_risks_traps: Treating intake cleanup as pure process hygiene and under-delivering on visible AI value; Over-claiming hard savings before finance attests; Extraction errors on non-standard terms if human confirmation is weakened; Requestor adoption failing so incomplete intake persists; Privilege leakage if source-system access is not fenced
gaps_in_current_moves_model: P3 does not yet compose a solution from multiple named building blocks; it tends to pick one archetype rather than bundle process + data + workflow + human-in-loop + controls; P4 struggles to keep operational-KPI value and hard-dollar value clearly separated with finance caveats; No native obligation-owner matrix artifact that P3/P5 can generate and P5 can enforce; P2 evidence intake assumes clean uploads; it has no strong path for defining required-field contracts per request type

business_outcome: Legal and business users can ask plain-language questions about signed contracts (What are our termination rights with this vendor? Which agreements cap liability?) and get accurate, cited answers in minutes instead of manual document hunting.
current_state_work_problem: Finding a clause today means someone remembers which agreement, opens the right file, and reads. Answers depend on individual memory, take hours, and are inconsistent. With contracts spread across 64 systems and 68 data sources, cross-contract questions are effectively unanswerable without a manual project.
phase_one_solution_approach: A knowledge and retrieval copilot over a governed set of signed contracts that answers questions with the exact clause and source document cited, scoped to what each user is permitted to see. It retrieves and summarizes; it does not give legal advice.
building_blocks: Data readiness/remediation; Knowledge/retrieval copilot; Controls/governance/risk
building_blocks_not_yet: AI-assisted decision support: Interpreting what a clause means for a decision is legal advice and must remain human-owned in phase one.; Workflow automation: This use case is answering questions, not moving work; automation adds risk without phase-one value.; System/platform implementation: A retrieval copilot over existing content does not require a new platform build yet.
required_p2_evidence: Inventory of signed contracts and where they live; Document access and permission rules by role; Privilege and confidentiality classification of documents; A set of real legal questions users ask today; Sample contracts with known correct answers for accuracy testing
p2_current_state_focus: Map where contract documents actually live, how clean and complete that set is, who is allowed to see what, and which questions users most need answered. Identify privileged or restricted content that must be excluded or fenced.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the retrieval copilot: which contract set is in scope, how answers cite the exact clause and source, how permissions are enforced per user, and how privileged content is kept out of general answers.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Value is time saved per legal question and faster response to business teams, framed as productivity (directional) rather than hard savings. Keep scope to a curated contract set to control cost and risk.
p5_execution_focus: Launch to a pilot group of attorneys and Legal Ops, measure answer accuracy and time saved, and expand the contract set only as accuracy and permission controls hold.
tower_metrics: Median time to answer a contract question; Answer accuracy rate against a verified test set; Percent of answers with a correct clause citation; Query volume and active users; Number of permission or privilege exceptions flagged
required_controls: Answers must cite the exact source clause and document; Permission-scoped retrieval so users only see allowed contracts; Privileged and confidential content excluded from general answers; Clear disclaimer that answers are informational, not legal advice; Audit log of questions and returned sources
client_stakeholders: Deputy General Counsel; Legal Operations Lead; Information Security; IT/Data owner; Records/Information Governance; OpCo legal and business users
what_good_looks_like: A user asks a contract question in plain language and gets a correct, cited answer in under a minute, with no ability to see contracts they are not entitled to, and attorneys trust it enough to use it as a first stop.
biggest_risks_traps: Confident but wrong answers (hallucinated clauses) eroding trust; Permission leakage exposing restricted or privileged contracts; Stale contract set giving answers from superseded versions; Users treating retrieved text as legal advice; Accuracy looking good in demo but degrading on messy real documents
gaps_in_current_moves_model: Moves has no native artifact for defining and enforcing document-level permission scoping in P3; P2 has no structured way to build a verified question/answer test set that P5 can measure accuracy against; P4 value modeling is weak for productivity-only use cases with no hard-dollar anchor; Retrieval accuracy and citation quality are not first-class Tower metrics the model knows how to define

business_outcome: No contract auto-renews on unfavorable terms or misses a notice deadline by surprise. Renewal and notice dates are known in advance, owned by a named person, and acted on deliberately.
current_state_work_problem: Renewal and notice obligations sit inside contracts with no reliable calendar and no clear owner. Combined with 320 obligation gaps, this creates silent risk: agreements auto-renew, notice windows close, and the business finds out too late. Tracking today is manual and incomplete.
phase_one_solution_approach: AI-assisted extraction of renewal and notice terms (dates, notice periods, auto-renewal flags) that a human confirms, loaded into a tracked calendar with a named owner per obligation, plus an operating cadence that surfaces upcoming and at-risk items before deadlines.
building_blocks: Data readiness/remediation; Human-in-the-loop agent; Workflow automation; Controls/governance/risk; Value tracking/operating cadence
building_blocks_not_yet: AI-assisted decision support: Whether to renew, renegotiate, or terminate is a business and legal decision; AI surfaces the deadline, humans decide.; Analytics/intelligence layer: Portfolio-level renewal analytics come after a clean, owned renewal record exists; not phase one.; System/platform implementation: A tracked calendar and cadence can be delivered without a new platform; broad orchestration was rejected for now.
required_p2_evidence: Contracts with renewal and notice terms for the pilot set; Current renewal calendar or tracker, however partial; Obligation gap register showing unowned renewal/termination items; Examples of past missed or near-missed renewals and their cost; Owner assignment rules by contract type and OpCo
p2_current_state_focus: Determine how renewals and notices are tracked today, where the gaps are, and what past misses have cost or risked. Confirm which contract types carry the most renewal exposure.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the extract-confirm-track flow: how renewal and notice terms are pulled and human-verified, how each gets a named owner, how alerts fire ahead of deadlines, and how exceptions escalate.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Value framed as risk reduction and prevented leakage from missed notices or unfavorable auto-renewals, treated as candidate value that becomes hard only after a documented avoided event. Modest phase-one scope tied to highest-risk contract types.
p5_execution_focus: Stand up the tracked calendar for the pilot contract set, assign owners, run the deadline cadence, and measure notice-risk reduction and on-time action rate.
tower_metrics: Renewal-notice risk count (upcoming windows without an owner or action); Obligation-owner completeness for renewal/notice terms; On-time notice action rate; Number of avoided unfavorable auto-renewals (evidenced); Aged/at-risk renewal items
required_controls: Human confirmation of every extracted renewal/notice term; Named owner required for each tracked obligation; Escalation path for approaching deadlines; Audit trail of notices, actions, and decisions; No automated renewal or termination action taken by AI
client_stakeholders: Deputy General Counsel; Legal Operations Lead; Procurement; Finance Controls; OpCo contract owners; Vendor management
what_good_looks_like: Every high-value contract has known renewal and notice dates, a named owner, and timely alerts; the business chooses renewals deliberately, and missed-notice surprises stop happening.
biggest_risks_traps: Extraction errors on notice periods creating false confidence; Owners assigned on paper but not actually acting; Booking risk-reduction value as hard savings before an avoided event is documented; Incomplete contract set leaving blind spots; Alert fatigue if thresholds are poorly tuned
gaps_in_current_moves_model: No native calendar/deadline-tracking artifact that P3 designs and P5 operates; P4 lacks a clean model for candidate risk-reduction value that converts to hard value only on an evidenced event; Owner-accountability enforcement (assigned vs actually acting) is not something P5 tracks natively; P2 has no structured capture for historical near-miss/loss events to anchor risk value

business_outcome: Contract terms that deviate from policy (liability caps, indemnity, data terms, non-standard clauses) are caught early, routed to the right approver, and resolved with a clear record, so exceptions are governed rather than slipping through.
current_state_work_problem: There are 360 policy exceptions in the evidence with inconsistent detection and routing. Non-standard terms are caught by whoever happens to notice, approvals are informal, and there is no reliable record of what was granted and why. This is a control and governance gap, not just a speed problem.
phase_one_solution_approach: An AI check that flags likely policy deviations against a defined policy standard and routes each flagged item to the correct approver with the relevant clause and policy reference, recording the decision. AI flags and routes; it never approves the exception itself.
building_blocks: Controls/governance/risk; Human-in-the-loop agent; Workflow automation; Data readiness/remediation
building_blocks_not_yet: AI-assisted decision support: Recommending whether to grant an exception edges into legal judgment; phase one flags and routes, humans decide and approve.; Analytics/intelligence layer: Exception-pattern analytics require a clean, categorized exception record first; premature in phase one.; System/platform implementation: Exception detection and routing can ride existing workflow tooling; no new platform in phase one.
required_p2_evidence: Written policy standard defining standard vs non-standard terms; Policy exception log with exception type and disposition; Current approval authority matrix (who can approve which exception); Examples of clauses that should trigger an exception; Routing rules and current escalation practice
p2_current_state_focus: Establish what counts as a policy exception, how they are detected and approved today, who holds approval authority, and where the current process is inconsistent or undocumented.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the deviation-detection check against the policy standard, the routing to the correct approver by exception type, the recorded-decision step, and the escalation path, all with a human approval gate.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Value framed as control strengthening and reduced governance risk (fewer ungoverned exceptions), largely directional and risk-reduction; keep scope to the highest-risk exception types.
p5_execution_focus: Roll out detection and routing for the pilot exception types, confirm approvals are consistently recorded, and measure exception-handling completeness and cycle time.
tower_metrics: Percent of exceptions detected and routed vs missed; Exception approval cycle time; Percent of exceptions with a recorded, authorized approval; Volume of exceptions by type; Number of ungoverned exceptions found after signature
required_controls: AI may flag and route but never approve an exception; Approval strictly by the authorized approver per policy; Every exception decision recorded with rationale; Audit trail of detection, routing, and approval; Policy standard versioned and change-controlled
client_stakeholders: Deputy General Counsel; Legal Operations Lead; Compliance/Governance; Finance Controls; Information Security; Procurement
what_good_looks_like: Non-standard terms are reliably caught, routed to the right approver, and resolved with a clear record; exceptions become a governed, auditable process instead of ad-hoc judgment calls.
biggest_risks_traps: Missed detections creating false assurance that all exceptions are caught; AI drifting toward implicitly approving by pre-filling decisions; Policy standard too vague to detect against reliably; Over-flagging causing approver fatigue and rubber-stamping; Treating a control improvement as if it were hard savings
gaps_in_current_moves_model: No native approval-authority matrix artifact that P3 defines and P5 enforces; Moves does not natively encode a policy standard to detect deviations against; P4 has weak value modeling for control/governance improvements that are risk-reduction rather than dollar-saving; Detection precision/recall are not Tower metrics the model knows how to define or govern

use_case: Matter and outside-counsel intake and triage
business_outcome: Legal work sent to outside counsel is properly scoped, packaged, and triaged first, so only work that truly needs external review goes out, spend is controlled, and internal teams keep visibility over matters.
current_state_work_problem: Requests reach outside counsel with incomplete context, and low-value or triageable work is sent externally because there is no consistent internal intake and triage step. Outside-counsel avoidance is currently only directional, meaning the organization cannot yet see or control this spend systematically. This mirrors the same intake and triage weaknesses seen across Legal.
phase_one_solution_approach: A guided matter intake that captures scope and context, an AI-assisted triage that prepares a complete work packet and flags what can be handled internally versus needs outside counsel, and a human decision step where Legal approves the routing. AI prepares and recommends triage; attorneys decide.
building_blocks: Process redesign; Human-in-the-loop agent; Workflow automation; Value tracking/operating cadence; Controls/governance/risk
building_blocks_not_yet: AI-assisted decision support: Recommending legal strategy or handling approach is attorney judgment; phase one only triages and packages, it does not advise.; Analytics/intelligence layer: Outside-counsel spend analytics need a clean matter and invoice baseline first, which does not yet exist reliably.; System/platform implementation: Triage can be delivered on existing intake tooling; a matter-management platform build is out of phase-one scope.; Knowledge/retrieval copilot: Useful later to pull prior similar matters, but not essential to prove the intake-and-triage value in phase one.
required_p2_evidence: Matter intake requests and how they are routed today; Outside-counsel invoice and matter baseline; Definition of what can be handled internally vs externally; Examples of matters that should not have gone to outside counsel; Current triage and approval practice for external legal work
p2_current_state_focus: Establish how matters are intaken and routed to outside counsel today, what the external spend baseline actually is, and where work is sent out that could have been triaged internally. Confirm outside-counsel avoidance is directional until invoice evidence supports it.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the guided matter intake, the AI-prepared work packet, the internal-vs-external triage recommendation, and the human approval step that controls routing.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Value framed as outside-counsel triage-hour avoidance, explicitly directional and requiring matter-invoice evidence and legal approval before any hard-savings claim. Small pilot on the highest-volume matter types.
p5_execution_focus: Pilot the intake-and-triage flow on selected matter types, measure how much work is triaged internally and packet quality, and validate any avoidance against real invoices before claiming savings.
tower_metrics: Outside-counsel triage hours avoided (evidenced); Percent of matters triaged internally vs sent external; Matter intake completeness rate; Matter cycle time to routing decision; Outside-counsel spend against baseline
required_controls: Attorney approval of every internal-vs-external routing decision; AI recommends triage but never sends work externally on its own; Privilege and confidentiality preserved in matter packets; Audit trail of triage recommendations and decisions; Finance sign-off before any avoidance is booked as hard savings
client_stakeholders: Deputy General Counsel; Legal Operations Lead; Finance Controls; Procurement; Outside-counsel relationship owner; OpCo requestors
what_good_looks_like: Matters arrive well-scoped, get triaged consistently, and only genuinely external work goes to outside counsel with a complete packet, giving Legal control and Finance a credible line of sight on external spend.
biggest_risks_traps: Claiming outside-counsel savings before invoice evidence supports it; Triage misclassifying complex matters as internal and creating legal risk; Weak matter baseline making value impossible to prove; Attorney adoption resistance to a triage step; Privilege exposure in prepared packets
gaps_in_current_moves_model: P4 cannot yet cleanly hold a value lever that is directional-until-attested and convert it to hard value only on invoice evidence; P2 has no strong path to build an outside-counsel spend baseline from invoice data; Moves lacks a triage-decision artifact (internal vs external) that P3 designs and P5 measures; Weakest of the five for P2/P3 because the underlying matter and invoice evidence is the thinnest, so the model would over-generate confident structure on sparse data

business_outcome: Fewer invoices falling into manual exception queues across Lakeshore's operating companies, so shared-services AP clears invoices faster, captures more early-payment discounts, and reduces overtime and rework at month-end.
current_state_work_problem: A large share of supplier invoices stop for manual handling: purchase-order mismatches, missing goods-receipts, wrong tax or coding, duplicate submissions, and non-PO invoices routed to the wrong approver. Each operating company has slightly different tolerances and vendor master data, so AP analysts re-key, chase approvers, and email buyers repeatedly. The team cannot easily see which exception types are the biggest volume drivers or which operating companies and vendors generate them.
phase_one_solution_approach: Start read-only: categorize and rank exception reasons from real AP data, standardize match tolerances and coding rules across operating companies, and give analysts a retrieval copilot that assembles the PO, receipt, and prior-invoice context on one screen so they resolve faster. Automate only the safe, deterministic paths (clear duplicates, exact three-way matches within tolerance) with a human confirming before any payment-affecting action.
building_blocks: Process redesign; Data readiness/remediation; Knowledge/retrieval copilot; Workflow automation; Value tracking/operating cadence
building_blocks_not_yet: AI-assisted decision support: Recommending how to resolve a coding or matching exception affects payments and tax; needs a proven baseline and human sign-off before AI suggestions are trusted.; Human-in-the-loop agent: An agent that acts on exceptions is only safe after the deterministic automation and control gates are proven in phase one.
required_p2_evidence: 12+ months of AP invoice and exception-queue extract with reason codes; Three-way match tolerance rules per operating company; Vendor master and duplicate-detection rules; Chart of accounts and coding/tax rules; Current approver routing and non-PO handling rules; Volume and cycle-time by exception type and operating company
p2_current_state_focus: Quantify exception volume, mix, and cycle time by reason, operating company, and vendor; expose where tolerances, vendor data, and routing rules diverge; size the discount leakage and rework cost.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design standardized tolerances and coding rules, the analyst copilot experience, and a decision tree separating auto-clearable paths from human-required ones; define the confirmation gate before any payment-affecting change.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Sequence quick wins (duplicate suppression, clean three-way matches) ahead of harder non-PO redesign; build the business case on discount capture, reduced rework hours, and faster close.
p5_execution_focus: Run a weekly exception-reduction cadence: track first-pass yield, exception aging, and auto-clear rate per operating company; tune rules and expand automation scope as confidence grows.
tower_metrics: Exception rate (% of invoices requiring manual handling); First-pass match yield %; Average exception resolution cycle time; Auto-clear rate on eligible invoices; Early-payment discount capture %; Duplicate/erroneous payment rate
required_controls: Human confirmation before any payment-affecting change; Segregation of duties between exception resolution and payment release; Full audit trail of every auto-cleared and reclassified invoice; Tolerance/rule change approval by controller; Duplicate-payment safeguard
client_stakeholders: Shared-Services AP Manager; Corporate Controller; Operating-company Finance leads; Procurement/Buyer leads; Internal Audit; IT/ERP owner
what_good_looks_like: Exception rate and resolution time drop measurably, more invoices clear straight-through within tolerance, discount capture rises, and every automated action has a controller-approved rule and an audit trail — with analysts spending time on genuine judgment cases, not re-keying.
biggest_risks_traps: Automating a bad tolerance rule and pushing wrong payments straight through; Dirty vendor master creating false duplicates or missed real duplicates; Operating-company rule differences treated as errors rather than legitimate variance; Over-claiming savings before discount capture is actually realized
gaps_in_current_moves_model: P2 diagnosis depends on a clean, reason-coded AP extract; without it the current-state sizing is guesswork; P3 struggles to represent per-operating-company tolerance variance as configuration rather than a single global rule; P4 value math needs realized-discount and rework-hour baselines the model does not yet capture natively

business_outcome: Suppliers and internal requesters get accurate 'where is my payment' answers without an AP analyst manually researching each one, cutting inbound inquiry volume and freeing the team for higher-value work while improving supplier relationships.
current_state_work_problem: AP and shared-services mailboxes are flooded with payment-status questions from vendors and internal staff. Answering each one means an analyst looking across the ERP, the payment run, and email threads to reconstruct whether an invoice was received, is on hold, is scheduled, or was paid. Answers are slow and inconsistent, and the same vendors ask repeatedly because they have no self-service visibility.
phase_one_solution_approach: Deploy a retrieval copilot that composes a clear, plain-language status from trusted AP and payment data for an analyst to review and send, and stand up an internal knowledge base of standard responses. Automate only fully-resolved, low-sensitivity status replies (for example 'paid on date X, reference Y') behind a human check; keep any dispute, hold-reason, or bank-detail question with a person.
building_blocks: Knowledge/retrieval copilot; Process redesign; Workflow automation; Human-in-the-loop agent; Value tracking/operating cadence
building_blocks_not_yet: System/platform implementation: A full supplier self-service portal is a larger build; phase one deflects inquiries without committing to a new external-facing platform.; Controls/governance/risk: Governance is present but light-touch here; a heavier controls layer is only needed once outbound replies are automated at scale.
required_p2_evidence: Sample of payment-status inquiries with categories and volumes; Invoice, payment-run, and remittance data model; Current SLA and response-time metrics; List of statuses and what each means per operating company; Rules for which questions require a human (holds, disputes, bank changes); Vendor contact and identity-verification rules
p2_current_state_focus: Measure inquiry volume, mix, and handle time; identify how many are simple status lookups versus genuine exceptions; find where status data is fragmented across systems.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the trusted status lookup, the copilot answer format, the human-review gate, and the strict rules separating auto-answerable status from anything touching holds, disputes, or bank details.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Prioritize highest-volume simple inquiries first; build value case on deflected touches, faster response SLA, and analyst hours reclaimed; scope optional future self-service portal.
p5_execution_focus: Track deflection rate, response time, and reopen/escalation rate weekly; expand auto-answer scope only as accuracy holds; monitor for any misrouted sensitive requests.
tower_metrics: Inquiry deflection rate %; Average response time to status inquiries; Inquiry volume per 1,000 invoices; Auto-answer accuracy %; Escalation/reopen rate; Analyst hours spent on status research
required_controls: Human review before any automated outbound reply in early phases; Vendor identity verification before sharing payment details; Strict block on bank-detail and payment-change requests through this channel; Audit log of every answer sent; No exposure of internal hold reasons without approval
client_stakeholders: Shared-Services AP Manager; Vendor Relations/Procurement; Corporate Controller; IT/ERP owner; Information Security; Operating-company Finance leads
what_good_looks_like: Routine status questions are answered fast and consistently with a person only reviewing where needed; sensitive requests are firmly routed to humans and verified; inbound volume drops and supplier satisfaction improves without any bank-fraud exposure.
biggest_risks_traps: Social-engineering/payment-fraud attempts riding the status channel; Sharing payment or bank details with an unverified requester; Confidently wrong status from stale or partial data; Deflecting a real dispute that needed human attention
gaps_in_current_moves_model: P3 must model a hard human-only boundary for fraud-sensitive requests; the current model tends toward maximizing automation, not fencing it; P2 evidence for identity-verification and fraud rules is not a standard input the model asks for; P4 value case for pure deflection (touches avoided) is weaker to quantify than hard-dollar savings and the model under-supports it

business_outcome: A faster, more predictable close across Lakeshore's operating companies, with fewer recurring issues, clearer ownership of blockers, and less last-minute firefighting by corporate accounting.
current_state_work_problem: The close is coordinated through spreadsheets, checklists, and email across many operating companies. Issues — late reconciliations, unexplained variances, intercompany mismatches, missing accruals — surface late and get tracked inconsistently. Corporate accounting cannot easily see, in real time, which entities are behind, which issues recur every month, and where the critical path is. Root causes are rarely captured, so the same problems repeat.
phase_one_solution_approach: Redesign the close as a tracked, structured workflow with clear owners, statuses, and dependencies; add an analytics layer that surfaces bottlenecks, recurring issue types, and at-risk entities; and give the close team a retrieval copilot that pulls prior-period notes and resolutions for a recurring issue. Keep judgment — accruals, variance explanations, sign-offs — firmly with accountants.
building_blocks: Process redesign; Workflow automation; Analytics/intelligence layer; Knowledge/retrieval copilot; Value tracking/operating cadence
building_blocks_not_yet: AI-assisted decision support: Suggesting accrual amounts or variance explanations touches the financial statements and audit; only appropriate after the tracked process and clean issue history exist.; Human-in-the-loop agent: An agent chasing or resolving close tasks needs a stable, well-owned workflow first, or it amplifies confusion during a time-critical period.
required_p2_evidence: Current close calendar and task checklist per operating company; Historical close-cycle timing and issue logs; List of recurring issue types and reconciliation break history; Intercompany matching process and known mismatch causes; Ownership/RACI for close tasks; Sign-off and controls documentation
p2_current_state_focus: Map the real close critical path, days-to-close by entity, and the recurring issue taxonomy; identify where handoffs and ownership break down.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the tracked close workflow, issue taxonomy, ownership model, and the bottleneck/risk analytics; define what stays human judgment versus what is coordination automation.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Target the entities and issue types driving the longest close; build value case on days-to-close reduction, fewer late adjustments, and reduced overtime.
p5_execution_focus: Run the close on the tracked cadence; review recurring-issue trends and critical-path slippage each cycle; drive root-cause fixes so repeat issues decline period over period.
tower_metrics: Days to close by entity and consolidated; Number and aging of open close issues; Recurring-issue recurrence rate; Late/post-close adjustment count; On-time task completion %; Intercompany mismatch count and clearing time
required_controls: Accountant sign-off retained on all judgment items; Segregation of duties on preparation vs. review vs. approval; Auditable trail of issue status and resolution; Change control on close checklist and workflow; No AI-authored journal entries in phase one
client_stakeholders: Corporate Controller; Assistant Controller / Close Manager; Operating-company accounting leads; Financial Reporting; Internal/External Audit liaison; IT/ERP owner
what_good_looks_like: The close runs on a live, owned tracker where blockers surface early, recurring issues visibly decline, days-to-close shortens, and accountants keep full control of judgment — with an auditable history of every issue and resolution.
biggest_risks_traps: Adding another tracker no one updates during crunch; Automating coordination while leaving root causes unfixed; Treating legitimate entity-level differences as issues; Any drift toward AI touching journal entries or estimates before it is safe
gaps_in_current_moves_model: P2 needs a structured recurring-issue history that most clients only hold in spreadsheets and email; the model has no clean way to ingest that today; P3 must express a coordination-only scope with a hard line at journal entries; the model tends to over-reach into 'decision support'; P4 days-to-close value is real but the model lacks a native baseline for close timing and adjustment counts

business_outcome: More reliable short-term cash forecasts across Lakeshore's operating companies, so treasury holds less idle buffer cash, borrows and invests more deliberately, and explains forecast misses with evidence rather than anecdote.
current_state_work_problem: Treasury builds consolidated cash forecasts from operating-company inputs of varying quality. Actuals routinely deviate from forecast, but the team cannot quickly attribute variance to its drivers — late AP runs, slipped AR collections, unexpected intercompany transfers, timing of tax or debt payments. Analysis is manual and backward-looking, so the same forecasting errors persist and treasury over-buffers to stay safe.
phase_one_solution_approach: Stand up an analytics layer that decomposes forecast-vs-actual variance by driver, entity, and category, and remediate the input data feeding the forecast so like is compared with like. Add a copilot to help analysts explain variance drivers from evidence. Keep the forecast itself, and any funding, borrowing, or investment decision, firmly human-owned; AI explains variance, it does not move money or set positions.
building_blocks: Analytics/intelligence layer; Data readiness/remediation; Knowledge/retrieval copilot; Process redesign; Value tracking/operating cadence
building_blocks_not_yet: AI-assisted decision support: AI-suggested forecast adjustments or funding actions carry direct financial and liquidity risk; only appropriate once variance drivers are well understood and trusted.; Workflow automation: Automating cash moves or forecast submissions is unsafe until input quality and variance attribution are proven; premature automation would propagate bad numbers.
required_p2_evidence: Historical cash forecasts vs. actuals by entity and category; Operating-company input methods and cadence; AP/AR timing data and payment-run calendars; Debt, tax, and intercompany transfer schedules; Bank balance and statement data; Documented forecast assumptions and known variance sources
p2_current_state_focus: Decompose historical variance by driver and entity; expose which inputs are unreliable and which categories drive the largest and most persistent misses; quantify the cost of over-buffering.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the variance-attribution analytics, the input-remediation approach, and the analyst copilot; define the strict boundary that AI explains variance and never proposes or executes cash actions.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Prioritize the entities and categories with the largest recurring variance; build value case on reduced buffer cash, better borrowing/investing timing, and improved forecast accuracy.
p5_execution_focus: Review forecast accuracy and variance drivers each cycle; feed lessons back into input quality and assumptions; track buffer reduction as accuracy improves.
tower_metrics: Forecast accuracy / mean absolute variance %; Variance attributable vs. unexplained %; Idle buffer cash held; Input timeliness and completeness by entity; Forecast miss frequency by category; Days of variance-analysis effort per cycle
required_controls: No AI execution of any cash, funding, or investment action; Human ownership and sign-off of the forecast; Auditable trail of variance analysis and input changes; Segregation between analysis and treasury execution; Approved data sources for bank and balance data
client_stakeholders: Corporate Treasurer; Assistant Treasurer / Cash Manager; Treasury Analysts; Operating-company Finance leads; Corporate Controller; IT/Treasury-systems owner
what_good_looks_like: Forecast variance is decomposed to its real drivers each cycle, input quality visibly improves, forecast accuracy rises, and treasury safely reduces idle buffer — with every cash decision still made by a person on better evidence.
biggest_risks_traps: Treating a variance-explanation tool as if it can predict or set cash positions; Bad operating-company inputs producing confident but wrong attribution; Reducing buffer too aggressively and risking a liquidity shortfall; Any AI path that could initiate a cash movement
gaps_in_current_moves_model: P2 variance decomposition needs granular forecast-vs-actual history with driver tagging that few clients hold cleanly; the model cannot manufacture it; P3 must enforce a hard 'explain-not-execute' liquidity boundary the model does not natively encode; P4 value (buffer reduction) requires a defensible liquidity-risk view the model has no way to represent, risking over-claimed savings

use_case: Duplicate and erroneous payment prevention (pre-pay controls)
business_outcome: Fewer dollars leaving Lakeshore in error — duplicate invoices, overpayments, wrong-vendor and fraudulent payments caught before the payment run rather than recovered painfully afterward — protecting cash and reducing recovery effort.
current_state_work_problem: Across operating companies with different vendor masters and approval habits, duplicates and overpayments slip through: same invoice submitted twice in different formats, PO and non-PO versions of one bill, fuzzy vendor-name variants, and occasional fraudulent or altered bank details. Today detection is partly after-the-fact via audits and vendor credits, and post-payment recovery is slow and incomplete.
phase_one_solution_approach: Remediate vendor master data, then add an analytics/controls layer that scores each invoice for duplicate and anomaly risk before the payment run, presenting flagged items to an AP reviewer with the matching evidence. All holds and releases stay human-decided; the system flags and explains, a person clears or blocks. No automated release of flagged payments in phase one.
building_blocks: Data readiness/remediation; Analytics/intelligence layer; Controls/governance/risk; Human-in-the-loop agent; Value tracking/operating cadence
building_blocks_not_yet: Workflow automation: Auto-releasing or auto-holding payments without human review is too risky early; a wrong auto-hold delays legitimate suppliers and a wrong release loses cash.; AI-assisted decision support: Recommending a pay/no-pay decision is a payment-integrity call that must be human-owned until detection accuracy and false-positive rates are proven.
required_p2_evidence: Vendor master with known duplicate/variant issues; Historical duplicate and overpayment recovery data; Invoice and payment-run history; Bank-detail change history and controls; Existing pre-pay control and approval rules; Known fraud or attempted-fraud incident records
p2_current_state_focus: Quantify duplicate/overpayment leakage and recovery lag; assess vendor-master quality and where variants hide; map current pre-pay controls and their gaps.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the risk-scoring and evidence-presentation experience, the reviewer workflow, and the control gates; explicitly keep pay/no-pay and hold/release as human decisions with tuned false-positive limits.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Prioritize highest-leakage vendors and operating companies; build value case on prevented erroneous payments and reduced recovery cost, net of reviewer effort.
p5_execution_focus: Track prevented payments, false-positive rate, and reviewer throughput each cycle; tune scoring to protect suppliers from over-holding while catching real errors.
tower_metrics: Duplicate/erroneous payment rate; Dollars prevented pre-payment; Detection false-positive rate; Post-payment recovery volume (should fall); Flag-to-clear cycle time; Vendor-master duplicate/variant count
required_controls: Human decision on every hold and release; Segregation of duties between flagging, review, and payment release; Bank-detail change verification and dual approval; Audit trail of every flag, override, and clearance; False-positive threshold governance to avoid unfair supplier holds
client_stakeholders: Corporate Controller; Shared-Services AP Manager; Internal Audit; Treasury (payment release); Information Security/Fraud; Operating-company Finance leads; IT/ERP owner
what_good_looks_like: Risky payments are flagged with clear evidence before money moves, a reviewer decides every hold and release, prevented-loss dollars are visible and rising, post-payment recoveries fall, and legitimate suppliers are rarely delayed by false positives.
biggest_risks_traps: False positives holding legitimate suppliers and damaging relationships; Missing a real duplicate because vendor variants weren't reconciled; Over-trusting the score and letting a human rubber-stamp releases; Any automation that releases a flagged payment without review; Fraud adapting faster than the rules
gaps_in_current_moves_model: P2 leakage sizing depends on recovery and near-miss data clients rarely capture cleanly; the model cannot infer it; P3 must model a strict pre-pay human-decision gate and a false-positive tolerance the current model does not express as a first-class control; P4 prevented-loss value is inherently a 'losses avoided' number that is harder to bank and easy to over-claim, and the model gives little guidance on defending it

business_outcome: Cut the volume and cost of routine IT tickets across Lakeshore's operating companies by letting employees self-resolve common requests (password issues, VPN, software install, how-to questions) with a trusted assistant, freeing service desk agents for complex work and shortening wait times.
current_state_work_problem: Each operating company runs its own service desk with inconsistent tooling and knowledge. A large share of tickets are repetitive, low-complexity questions already answered somewhere in scattered runbooks, intranet pages, and agents' heads. Employees can't find answers, so they open tickets; agents copy-paste the same responses; knowledge is stale and duplicated across companies.
phase_one_solution_approach: Stand up a knowledge assistant that answers the top repetitive question categories using vetted, current IT knowledge content, with clear handoff to a human agent when it is unsure or the issue is sensitive. Start read-only and advisory: it suggests answers and self-service steps, it does not change any system on the employee's behalf yet.
building_blocks: Knowledge/retrieval copilot; Data readiness/remediation; Human-in-the-loop agent; Analytics/intelligence layer; Value tracking/operating cadence
building_blocks_not_yet: Workflow automation: Auto-executing fixes (e.g., resetting passwords or provisioning) crosses into changing live systems; not safe until deflection accuracy and knowledge quality are proven and identity controls are wired in.; System/platform implementation: Consolidating operating companies onto one service desk platform is a larger program; Phase 1 rides on existing tools to prove value fast.
required_p2_evidence: 12 months of ticket history categorized by topic, volume, resolution time, and reopen rate across operating companies; Inventory of current knowledge sources (runbooks, intranet, macros) with owner and last-updated date; Top 20 repetitive request categories and their current fully-loaded handling cost; Baseline first-contact resolution and average handle time per company; List of question types that must always route to a human (security, HR-adjacent, executive)
p2_current_state_focus: Quantify how many tickets are genuinely deflectable, where the answers already live, how stale and fragmented the knowledge is, and which categories carry the most repetitive load and cost per operating company.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the answer scope (which categories are in-bounds), the confidence threshold for handing off to a human, the knowledge-refresh model, and the employee experience across companies with different tooling.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Build the deflection business case: expected deflection rate per category, agent hours freed, phased rollout by operating company, and the knowledge-maintenance operating cost that must be funded to keep it accurate.
p5_execution_focus: Run a weekly cadence on deflection rate, answer accuracy, escalation quality, and employee satisfaction; retire and refresh stale knowledge; expand category coverage only as accuracy holds.
tower_metrics: Deflection rate (share of eligible tickets self-resolved); Cost avoided per month from deflected tickets; First-contact resolution rate; Answer accuracy / correction rate; Employee satisfaction with self-service
required_controls: Answers restricted to vetted, owned knowledge sources with visible citations; Guaranteed human handoff for security, HR-adjacent, and low-confidence cases; No account or system changes performed automatically in Phase 1; Content review and freshness owner for every knowledge source; Audit trail of what was answered and where the employee went next
client_stakeholders: Corporate IT service desk lead; Operating-company IT managers; Knowledge management owner; Information security lead; HR / employee experience partner
what_good_looks_like: Employees get an accurate, cited answer in seconds for common issues, ticket volume for repetitive categories drops measurably, agents spend their time on complex work, and knowledge stays current because ownership and a refresh cadence are funded.
biggest_risks_traps: Confidently wrong answers erode trust and quietly increase rework; Stale knowledge poisons deflection; if no one owns refresh, accuracy decays; Deflection is claimed but tickets just shift channel or reopen later; Fragmented tooling across operating companies makes one experience hard; Measuring 'tickets touched' instead of genuinely resolved inflates the story
gaps_in_current_moves_model: No first-class notion of a funded knowledge-freshness owner as an ongoing operating cost; Deflection value is easy to overstate without a rigorous 'genuinely resolved vs. reopened' definition baked into value tracking; Model doesn't yet standardize a per-operating-company rollout ledger for holdco structures

business_outcome: Make getting the right application access faster and safer: requests are understood, routed to the correct approver with full context, and granted only after human approval, reducing wait times and access-related audit findings across Lakeshore's operating companies.
current_state_work_problem: Access requests flow through email, tickets, and spreadsheets with unclear ownership of who approves what. Employees don't know what to ask for, approvers lack context to decide, and joiner/mover/leaver changes lag. The result is slow onboarding, over-provisioned access, and painful audits because entitlements and approvals aren't consistently recorded.
phase_one_solution_approach: Assist and orchestrate the request-and-approval workflow without auto-granting. The assistant helps the employee request the right access, assembles context (role, manager, existing access, risk level) for the approver, routes to the correct approver, and records the decision. Every grant still requires an explicit human approval; high-risk and privileged access always escalates.
building_blocks: Workflow automation; AI-assisted decision support; Human-in-the-loop agent; Controls/governance/risk; Data readiness/remediation
building_blocks_not_yet: System/platform implementation: A full identity-governance platform rollout is a larger program; Phase 1 orchestrates and records on top of existing systems to prove flow and control first.; Value tracking/operating cadence: Introduced from Phase 4 once baseline cycle-time and audit-finding data exist; premature to run a value cadence before the workflow is trusted.
required_p2_evidence: Catalog of applications and their access levels, owners, and risk classification; Current request-to-grant cycle time and volume by application and company; Map of who actually approves what today vs. who should; Recent access-related audit findings and their root causes; Joiner/mover/leaver process documentation and current gaps
p2_current_state_focus: Expose how access is really requested, approved, and revoked today; where approver ownership is missing; how long grants take; and which gaps drive audit findings and over-provisioning.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the approval routing rules, the risk tiers that determine how much scrutiny a request gets, the context pack shown to approvers, and the strict boundary where automation stops and human approval is mandatory.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Business case on faster onboarding, reduced over-provisioning, and fewer audit findings; phased by application risk tier and operating company, with the control model as a non-negotiable dependency.
p5_execution_focus: Track cycle time, approval quality, and access-review completeness; run periodic recertification; expand automation scope only for low-risk access as trust is earned.
tower_metrics: Average request-to-grant cycle time; Share of requests routed to the correct approver first time; Access-related audit findings per period; Over-provisioned / unused entitlements identified and removed; On-time completion of access recertifications
required_controls: No automatic granting of access in Phase 1 — human approval required for every grant; Mandatory escalation for privileged, financial, and cross-company access; Separation of duties enforced in routing (requester cannot approve own request); Complete, tamper-evident record of request, context, approver, and decision; Least-privilege defaults and periodic recertification built in
client_stakeholders: Identity and access management lead; Information security / CISO office; Application owners across operating companies; Internal audit and compliance; HR (for joiner/mover/leaver triggers)
what_good_looks_like: New hires get productive access quickly, approvers decide with full context, privileged access is always scrutinized by a human, and auditors can trace every grant to a documented, appropriate approval — with over-provisioning steadily shrinking.
biggest_risks_traps: Auto-granting access to move faster is the single biggest control risk — must not happen in Phase 1; Bad or missing application/role data makes routing and context untrustworthy; Separation-of-duties gaps let requesters approve their own access; Speeding up grants without also tightening revocation worsens over-provisioning; Holdco complexity: cross-operating-company access blurs approver ownership
gaps_in_current_moves_model: Model needs a strong, explicit 'automation stops here' guardrail concept for control-sensitive workflows so auto-grant never leaks in; Separation-of-duties and recertification aren't first-class control primitives yet; Cross-entity (holdco) approver ownership isn't modeled — real risk for shared services serving many operating companies

business_outcome: Resolve IT incidents faster by giving responders an accurate, up-to-date summary of what's happening and routing each incident to the right team the first time, reducing bounce-backs, mean time to resolve, and business disruption for Lakeshore's operating companies.
current_state_work_problem: Incidents arrive with sparse or noisy descriptions and get mis-routed between teams, each re-reading history and re-diagnosing. During major incidents, status is assembled manually from chat threads and calls, so leadership and affected businesses get inconsistent updates. Time is lost to triage and context-rebuilding rather than fixing.
phase_one_solution_approach: Provide a drafting and routing assistant: it summarizes the incident from available signals, suggests the likely owning team and priority, and drafts a status update — all for a human responder to confirm. It accelerates triage and communication; it does not take remediation actions or close incidents on its own.
building_blocks: Knowledge/retrieval copilot; AI-assisted decision support; Workflow automation; Human-in-the-loop agent; Analytics/intelligence layer
building_blocks_not_yet: Controls/governance/risk: Lightweight guardrails apply, but heavy governance tooling isn't the Phase 1 driver since the assistant only drafts and suggests — no automated remediation to govern yet.; Value tracking/operating cadence: Comes online in Phase 4/5 once mean-time-to-resolve and mis-route baselines are established; a value cadence before then would track noise.
required_p2_evidence: Incident history with descriptions, routing paths, reassignment counts, and resolution times; Current team-ownership map and routing rules across operating companies; Sample major-incident timelines showing how status was communicated; Priority/severity definitions and how consistently they're applied; Sources available at incident time (monitoring, prior similar incidents, runbooks)
p2_current_state_focus: Measure how often incidents are mis-routed and reassigned, how much time is lost re-diagnosing, and how inconsistent major-incident communication is today.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design what a trustworthy summary must contain, the routing suggestion logic and confidence handling, the responder confirmation step, and the communication templates for major incidents.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Business case on reduced mean-time-to-resolve, fewer reassignments, and faster, consistent stakeholder communication; phased by incident type and operating company.
p5_execution_focus: Track routing accuracy, reassignment rate, and resolution time; feed resolved-incident learnings back into summaries and runbooks; expand coverage as accuracy holds.
tower_metrics: Mean time to resolve; First-time-correct routing rate; Average reassignments per incident; Major-incident communication timeliness; Responder-rated summary usefulness
required_controls: Responder confirms routing and priority before action — no auto-close or auto-remediation; Summaries cite their source signals so responders can verify; Clear labeling that updates are drafts pending human approval; Sensitive incidents (security, data exposure) follow a protected path; Full timeline record of suggestions, confirmations, and communications
client_stakeholders: IT operations / incident management lead; Major-incident commander role; Operating-company IT leads; Information security (for security incidents); Service owners for affected applications
what_good_looks_like: Responders open an incident to a clear, sourced summary and a sensible routing suggestion, spend their energy fixing rather than triaging, and leadership gets timely consistent updates during major incidents — with humans still owning every decision.
biggest_risks_traps: A confidently wrong summary sends responders down the wrong path faster; Over-trust: responders rubber-stamp routing suggestions without checking; Security incidents mishandled if they aren't carved onto a protected path; Garbage-in incident data makes summaries and routing unreliable; Measuring 'summaries generated' instead of resolution and routing accuracy
gaps_in_current_moves_model: No first-class 'protected/sensitive path' concept for incidents that must bypass the standard assistant flow; Model lacks a built-in feedback loop that turns resolved incidents into improved future summaries and runbooks; Real-time / time-critical operating cadence differs from the model's periodic-review default

business_outcome: Reduce IT cost and risk across Lakeshore's operating companies by building a trustworthy view of every application — cost, usage, overlap, and risk — and identifying candidates to retire, consolidate, or renegotiate, with decisions made by humans on solid evidence.
current_state_work_problem: After years of acquisitions, operating companies run overlapping applications with no single, current inventory. Spend is fragmented across contracts, real usage is unknown, and redundant tools persist because no one can see the whole picture. Rationalization stalls because the evidence to decide is scattered and stale.
phase_one_solution_approach: Assemble and analyze a governed application inventory: bring together cost, usage, ownership, overlap, and risk into one intelligence layer, and surface prioritized rationalization candidates with the evidence behind each. Recommendations are advisory — retire/consolidate decisions are made by application and business owners, not automatically.
building_blocks: Data readiness/remediation; Analytics/intelligence layer; AI-assisted decision support; Value tracking/operating cadence; Controls/governance/risk
building_blocks_not_yet: Workflow automation: Nothing should be decommissioned automatically; retirement is a deliberate, owner-approved change with migration and dependency risk.; System/platform implementation: Consolidating onto target platforms is a downstream program that follows the rationalization decisions, not a Phase 1 activity.
required_p2_evidence: Consolidated application inventory across operating companies with owners; Actual usage/adoption data per application (not just licenses purchased); Total cost per application including license, support, and infrastructure; Contract and renewal calendar with terms and exit clauses; Overlap map showing applications serving the same capability and their dependencies
p2_current_state_focus: Establish a single credible picture of what applications exist, what they truly cost, whether they're actually used, where they overlap, and what depends on them — replacing scattered, stale views.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the rationalization scoring (cost vs. usage vs. risk vs. overlap), the evidence pack per candidate, and the decision framework owners will use to choose retire / consolidate / renegotiate / keep.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Build a phased savings roadmap tied to contract renewal timing and dependency risk, quantifying cost-out per wave and the migration effort each retirement requires.
p5_execution_focus: Run an ongoing operating cadence that tracks realized savings against the plan, keeps the inventory current, and re-scores the portfolio as contracts and usage change.
tower_metrics: Applications retired or consolidated; Annual cost eliminated (realized vs. planned); Redundant-capability overlap reduced; Share of portfolio with current, trustworthy inventory data; License utilization rate
required_controls: No application decommissioned without owner and dependency sign-off; Every recommendation traceable to its cost, usage, and risk evidence; Business-continuity and data-retention checks before any retirement; Inventory data governed for freshness and accuracy with named owners; Change and migration plan required before a retire decision executes
client_stakeholders: CIO / IT finance (technology business management) lead; Application owners across operating companies; Enterprise architecture; Procurement / vendor management; Operating-company business sponsors
what_good_looks_like: Leadership sees one trustworthy portfolio view, rationalization candidates come with the evidence to decide, retirements happen safely with dependencies handled, and realized savings are tracked against the plan rather than assumed.
biggest_risks_traps: Stale or incomplete inventory data leads to wrong retire decisions; Counting license spend without real usage overstates savings; Retiring an app that a hidden downstream process depends on causes outages; 'Planned savings' declared as realized without a tracking cadence; Holdco politics: operating companies resist giving up 'their' tools
gaps_in_current_moves_model: Value tracking must distinguish planned vs. realized savings over time — easy to overstate at business-case stage; Dependency-risk modeling (what breaks if we retire this) isn't a first-class element; Cross-operating-company ownership and politics of shared/duplicated apps aren't modeled; Inventory freshness needs a funded ongoing owner, not a one-time data pull

business_outcome: Ensure every new hire is productive on day one and every departure is fully and promptly de-provisioned, by coordinating the many IT tasks behind joiner/mover/leaver events across Lakeshore's operating companies — cutting onboarding delays and closing the security gap left by incomplete offboarding.
current_state_work_problem: Onboarding and offboarding IT tasks (accounts, equipment, application access, group memberships) are tracked in checklists and emails that vary by operating company. New hires wait on missing access; more dangerously, leavers keep access for days or weeks because de-provisioning steps are missed, creating security and audit exposure. No one has a live view of completion.
phase_one_solution_approach: Orchestrate and track the joiner/mover/leaver task set from the HR trigger: the assistant generates the right task list per role and company, routes each task to the right owner, and tracks completion, flagging anything overdue — especially offboarding steps. Sensitive de-provisioning is executed by owners with confirmation, not silently automated, in Phase 1.
building_blocks: Workflow automation; Process redesign; Human-in-the-loop agent; Controls/governance/risk; Value tracking/operating cadence
building_blocks_not_yet: AI-assisted decision support: Phase 1 is mostly deterministic orchestration of known tasks; richer recommendation logic (e.g., role-based access suggestions) is a later enhancement.; System/platform implementation: A unified HR-to-IT provisioning platform across operating companies is a larger downstream program; Phase 1 coordinates across existing systems.
required_p2_evidence: Current joiner/mover/leaver task lists per role and operating company with owners; Time-to-productive-access for recent hires and gaps encountered; Time-to-full-deprovision for recent leavers and any lingering-access findings; HR trigger data quality and timeliness (are IT events fired reliably?); Audit findings related to orphaned accounts or excess retained access
p2_current_state_focus: Show how long onboarding really takes, how reliably offboarding completes, where tasks fall through the cracks, and how big the lingering-access security gap is across operating companies.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Redesign the joiner/mover/leaver task flow, define role-and-company task templates, set ownership and escalation for overdue tasks, and fix the boundary where sensitive de-provisioning requires confirmed human execution.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Business case on faster onboarding, eliminated lingering access, and reduced audit exposure; phased by operating company and by event type, with HR-trigger reliability as a key dependency.
p5_execution_focus: Track onboarding completeness, offboarding timeliness, and overdue-task rates; run recurring reviews to catch orphaned accounts; tighten automation for low-risk steps as trust grows.
tower_metrics: Time to productive access for new hires; Time to full de-provisioning for leavers; Offboarding completeness (share of leavers fully de-provisioned on time); Overdue onboarding/offboarding tasks; Orphaned/lingering-access findings per period
required_controls: Sensitive de-provisioning confirmed and recorded by an accountable owner, not silently automated in Phase 1; Hard escalation on overdue offboarding steps for departing employees; Complete audit trail linking each HR event to its completed IT tasks; Separation of duties between requesting and executing sensitive changes; Reliable, timely HR trigger as a governed dependency
client_stakeholders: HR shared services / HRIS lead; IT service desk and provisioning teams; Identity and access management lead; Information security / internal audit; Operating-company people managers
what_good_looks_like: A new hire has the right accounts, equipment, and access on day one; when someone leaves, all access is closed the same day with a clean audit trail; and leadership sees live completion status rather than discovering gaps at audit time.
biggest_risks_traps: Offboarding is the real risk: missed de-provisioning leaves live access for departed employees; Unreliable or late HR triggers mean the whole flow starts on bad data; Auto-executing sensitive de-provisioning without confirmation could disrupt the wrong person; Per-company task variation makes one orchestration model hard to standardize; Focusing on shiny onboarding while under-investing in unglamorous offboarding controls
gaps_in_current_moves_model: Model needs to treat an external trigger (HR event) reliability as a governed dependency, not an assumption; Time-critical offboarding SLAs differ from the model's periodic-review cadence default; Per-operating-company task-template variation isn't a first-class concept for holdco shared services; Separation of duties between requesting and executing sensitive changes isn't a built-in control primitive

business_outcome: New suppliers to Lakeshore's operating companies are onboarded faster and with consistent risk screening, so corporate shared services reduce onboarding cycle time and cut the number of high-risk vendors entering the base without proper review.
current_state_work_problem: Each operating company intakes vendors its own way, often by email and spreadsheet. Risk checks (financial health, insurance, sanctions/watchlist, cyber, conflict of interest) are inconsistent, and shared services can't see one clean picture of who is being onboarded, how long it takes, or which checks were skipped. Duplicate vendor records proliferate across operating companies.
phase_one_solution_approach: Stand up one intake front door and a standardized risk-review checklist for corporate shared services, with a copilot that drafts the risk summary from submitted documents and screening results. A procurement analyst always reviews and signs off before a vendor is approved. No auto-approval in phase one.
building_blocks: Process redesign; Knowledge/retrieval copilot; Human-in-the-loop agent; Controls/governance/risk; Value tracking/operating cadence
building_blocks_not_yet: Workflow automation: Full straight-through automation of approvals is unsafe until the standardized checklist and human review are proven stable; automate routing only after the manual path is trusted.; System/platform implementation: Replacing or consolidating vendor master systems across operating companies is a large program; phase one runs on top of existing systems rather than replacing them.; Data readiness/remediation: Deep vendor-master de-duplication across all operating companies is a heavy remediation effort better scoped as its own move once intake is standardized.
required_p2_evidence: Current intake volumes and cycle time per operating company; Existing risk-check steps and which are actually performed today; Sample of recent vendor onboardings with documents and outcomes; List of screening data sources available (financial, sanctions, cyber) and their coverage; Count and examples of duplicate vendor records across operating companies
p2_current_state_focus: Map how each operating company intakes and screens vendors today, quantify cycle time and rework, and identify where risk checks are inconsistent or skipped.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the single intake form, the standardized risk checklist, the copilot-drafted risk summary, and the review/approval workflow with clear human sign-off points.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Build the business case on cycle-time reduction, fewer high-risk vendors admitted, and analyst time saved; sequence rollout operating-company by operating-company.
p5_execution_focus: Run the standardized intake live for pilot operating companies, track sign-off quality, and hold a regular operating cadence on onboarding volume, risk flags, and exceptions.
tower_metrics: Average vendor onboarding cycle time; Percent of intakes with complete risk screening; Number of high-risk vendors flagged before approval; Analyst hours per vendor onboarded; Duplicate vendor records prevented
required_controls: Mandatory human sign-off before any vendor is approved; Audit trail of every screening result and reviewer decision; Segregation between the analyst who prepares and the approver who signs off; Handling rules for sensitive supplier financial and personal data; Escalation path for high-risk or watchlist matches
client_stakeholders: Corporate VP of Procurement / Shared Services; Category and vendor management leads; Risk and compliance officer; Operating-company procurement contacts; Legal (for conflict-of-interest and sanctions escalations)
what_good_looks_like: One clean intake front door where any operating company submits a vendor, a consistent risk summary is drafted in minutes, an analyst reviews and signs off, and shared services can see onboarding volume, cycle time, and risk flags in one place.
biggest_risks_traps: Screening data sources may be incomplete or stale, giving false comfort on risk; Operating companies resist a central front door and keep shadow intake processes; Copilot risk summaries could be over-trusted and reduce genuine analyst scrutiny; Duplicate and messy vendor data undermines a clean single view
gaps_in_current_moves_model: Moves model does not yet specify how external screening data sources are connected and their coverage verified; No built-in pattern for a de-duplication effort that runs alongside a live intake process; Limited guidance on how the copilot's confidence is shown so reviewers don't over-trust it

business_outcome: Statements of work across operating companies are reviewed faster and hold to Lakeshore's standard terms, so corporate shared services reduce off-standard clauses, contain unpriced scope, and lower contract risk before signature.
current_state_work_problem: SOWs arrive in many formats and are reviewed manually by whoever is available. Standard terms (rate cards, liability, data protection, deliverable acceptance) are enforced inconsistently. Reviewers miss non-standard clauses and scope that isn't tied to a price, and there is no easy way to see how often SOWs deviate from policy.
phase_one_solution_approach: A review copilot reads a submitted SOW, compares it against Lakeshore's standard-terms playbook, and drafts a flag list of deviations and missing clauses for a procurement or legal reviewer. The reviewer decides; the tool never approves or edits the contract on its own. Ties into AbarVa's Source surface where the SOW originates from a sourcing event.
building_blocks: Process redesign; Knowledge/retrieval copilot; AI-assisted decision support; Human-in-the-loop agent; Controls/governance/risk
building_blocks_not_yet: Workflow automation: Auto-routing and auto-clearing of clean SOWs should wait until the deviation-flagging quality is proven against reviewer judgment.; System/platform implementation: Deep integration into a contract lifecycle system is a later step; phase one works from submitted documents.; Value tracking/operating cadence: A regular value cadence is valuable but secondary until the review flow itself is trusted; add once deviation rates are measurable.
required_p2_evidence: Lakeshore's current standard-terms playbook and rate-card policy; Sample of recent SOWs across operating companies with review notes; Typical review turnaround time and reviewer workload; Examples of past disputes or overruns traced to weak SOW terms; How SOWs connect to sourcing events in Source today
p2_current_state_focus: Understand how SOWs are reviewed today, where standard terms are and aren't enforced, and which deviations cause the most downstream cost or risk.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the standard-terms playbook the copilot checks against, the deviation flag format, and the reviewer decision workflow with legal escalation.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Justify the move on faster review turnaround, fewer off-standard clauses signed, and reduced unpriced scope; sequence by SOW volume per category.
p5_execution_focus: Run copilot-assisted review live for pilot categories, track reviewer agreement with flags, and refine the playbook based on real deviations.
tower_metrics: Average SOW review turnaround time; Percent of SOWs with all standard terms present; Number of off-standard clauses caught before signature; Reviewer hours per SOW; Value of unpriced scope identified and closed
required_controls: Human reviewer decision required on every flagged deviation; Legal escalation path for high-risk clauses; Version-controlled standard-terms playbook with owner; Audit trail linking each flag to a reviewer decision; Confidentiality handling for supplier contract terms
client_stakeholders: Corporate VP of Procurement / Shared Services; Category managers; Legal / contracts counsel; Operating-company procurement leads; Finance (for rate-card and pricing policy)
what_good_looks_like: A reviewer opens a SOW and immediately sees a clear, cited list of where it deviates from Lakeshore's standard terms and what scope isn't priced, decides quickly, and shared services can see deviation rates across operating companies.
biggest_risks_traps: The copilot may miss subtle or novel clauses that a seasoned reviewer would catch; An outdated standard-terms playbook produces misleading flags; Reviewers may rubber-stamp the flag list instead of exercising judgment; Legal may distrust the tool without clear evidence of accuracy
gaps_in_current_moves_model: Moves model lacks a clear pattern for keeping the standard-terms playbook current and owned; No defined handoff between Source sourcing events and SOW review beyond narrative; Limited guidance on measuring copilot flag accuracy against legal judgment over time

business_outcome: Lakeshore's corporate shared services see every upcoming contract renewal across operating companies early enough to act, so fewer contracts auto-renew unmanaged, more are competitively sourced or renegotiated, and savings are captured that would otherwise be lost.
current_state_work_problem: Renewal dates live scattered in spreadsheets, inboxes, and individual heads across operating companies. Contracts frequently auto-renew because no one saw the deadline in time, forfeiting the chance to renegotiate or re-source. There is no single forward-looking view of the renewal pipeline or its value at stake.
phase_one_solution_approach: Build one consolidated renewal calendar and an intelligence layer that surfaces upcoming renewals ranked by value and negotiation leverage, with recommended actions (renegotiate, re-source, consolidate, let lapse). A procurement lead decides on each; the tool recommends but never triggers a renewal or notice on its own. Feeds candidates into AbarVa's Source surface for competitive events and Tower for value tracking.
building_blocks: Data readiness/remediation; Analytics/intelligence layer; AI-assisted decision support; Human-in-the-loop agent; Value tracking/operating cadence
building_blocks_not_yet: Workflow automation: Automatically issuing renewal or non-renewal notices carries real contractual and financial consequences and must stay a human decision in phase one.; Knowledge/retrieval copilot: A negotiation copilot is valuable later but depends first on a clean, complete renewal dataset; sequence it after the pipeline view is trusted.; Controls/governance/risk: Governance controls are lighter here than in intake or SOW review; add formal controls once actions on renewals are taken at scale.
required_p2_evidence: Inventory of active contracts with renewal dates and notice periods across operating companies; Annual spend and value at stake per contract; History of contracts that auto-renewed unmanaged and the missed-savings estimate; Which renewals were competitively sourced vs rolled over last year; Data quality and completeness of existing contract records
p2_current_state_focus: Assemble a complete, trustworthy view of upcoming renewals and quantify how much value is lost today to unmanaged auto-renewals.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the consolidated renewal calendar, the ranking of renewals by value and leverage, and the recommended-action logic with a human decision point.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Size savings from proactively managed renewals versus the auto-renew baseline; prioritize the highest-value, highest-leverage renewals first.
